blocks.text: Whole people. Lasting impact.

MedWHOLE Alliance for Health and Development is a Nigerian non-profit working to restore people and communities through free education, free healthcare and skills training. Our work began in 2021 in Gosa, on the Nnamdi Azikiwe Airport Road in Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja.

blocks.text: MedWHOLE Academy
Whole child. Whole family. Whole community.

The Academy is our largest and longest-running work. It provides free education for children and teenagers in Gosa and Kunyami: holiday lessons every August, a capacity building club that meets weekly through the year, scholarships for out of school children, and coaching for the exams that decide what comes next.
It began in 2021 with twenty-one children. This August it taught more than seven hundred across two communities.

items: 450 children at Summer School Gosa, August 2026
280 a day at Kunyami, in its first year

blocks.text: Our other work
Alongside the Academy, we run free medical outreaches in communities without health facilities, and we train young adults who have volunteered with us.
The two connect. The volunteers who staffed our February outreach in Kunyami became the first cohort of our skills programme, and twelve of them completed it in June.

items: Health — medical outreaches, school health screening, nutrition, and follow-up care after referral
Empowerment — skills training, mentorship, and a community innovation challenge with grant funding

blocks.text: Seven referrals, seven recoveries

At a free outreach in Kunyami in February, seven people were found to need surgery. Each was referred to Gibonna Women's Hospital in Garki, where all seven operations were carried out. All seven recovered without complications.
Identifying a case takes a morning. Following it through to recovery takes months, and it is the part that decides whether an outreach mattered.
Three pillars, pursued together

Health, literacy and empowerment are not separate problems, so we do not treat them separately. A child who cannot see the board does not need a better teacher. A mother who cannot read a prescription has not really been treated.
We call our method the Made Whole Journey. Every programme is built to move through four phases — engaged, equipped, deployed, supported — and we judge each one by how far it actually gets.
Where we work
Where our work began: Gosa, Kunyami and Toge, in Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja.
Our first community, and where everything was built. Five years of a free Summer School programme, free health outreaches, and an innovation challenge run by Gosa's own young adults.
A farming community of more than three thousand, with no health facility of its own. In one year we opened a weekly club, a summer school and a skills cohort here.
Around four thousand people, a few primary schools, no secondary school and no hospital. We began with school health in June 2026 and are working out what comes next with the people who live there.
Gosa, Kunyami and Toge are where we started. We have begun work in other communities, and each one gets a page here once there is enough behind it to say something true.

blocks.text: Who we are

A Nigerian non-profit restoring people and communities, and staying long enough for the change to hold. Our work began in 2021 in Gosa, on the Nnamdi Azikiwe Airport Road in Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja.
We do not think a person is a single problem to be solved. Health, learning and livelihood arrive together in people's lives, so we work on them together, in the same communities, year after year.
That conviction is the organisation. Everything else on this page — the three pillars, the method, the governance, the figures below — is how we act on it and how we hold ourselves to it.
So far

items: 700+ children at Summer School this August
12 young adults through a full skills cohort

blocks.text: MedWHOLE Alliance for Health and Development is a registered Nigerian non-profit. Our work began in 2021 in Gosa, a community on the Airport Road outside Abuja, with a weekly club for twenty-one children. Today we run education, health and empowerment programmes in Gosa, Kunyami and Toge. These are our first communities.

Our work is held in three pillars — health, literacy and empowerment. Each pillar holds programmes. Each programme holds dated events that carry their own numbers. Every figure on this site can be traced down to a named community on a named day.

items: 700+ children at Summer School in August 2026

blocks.text: What we mean by whole

Need rarely arrives one problem at a time. A family short of money for school fees is usually also a family that cannot easily reach a clinic. So we work on more than one thing at once, and we stay long enough to see what changes.

In practice that looks ordinary. A summer school timetable carries mathematics and reading in the morning, a skills lab in the afternoon, and a health talk midweek. The Health Service team runs deworming inside an education programme. The volunteers who staff a medical outreach become the next cohort of a skills course.
Vision, mission and belief

items: Our vision — A society transformed by whole individuals who serve as lights within their communities.

Our mission — To improve human development through faith-centred engagement in health, literacy and empowerment, guiding individuals through discipleship and deployment toward sustainable community impact.
What we believe — Whole people create lasting impact.

blocks.text: We picture communities where people are not only supported but equipped — where the people we have worked with become the leaders, teachers, carers and catalysts their own communities need.
So every pillar is pursued in full, every piece of work touches more than one part of a person's life, and everyone we work with is prepared to serve others in turn.

sections.label: What we believe, and how we work

blocks.text: What we believe, and how we work

Our work is motivated by Christian faith. It shows less in what we say than in how we work, and it has never decided who we serve. Our services are open to everyone, without condition and without regard to faith, background or belief.

Families hand us their children every August, and we keep that trust by asking first and keeping our word. When three parents in Toge declined deworming for their children, the refusals were written down and the children were not treated.

Free does not mean second-rate. When we screened 196 pupils at Toge, we measured them against the standard the World Health Organization uses for school-age children, the same one a well-funded clinic would use.

And we say what we cannot count. Our Toge figures came with a plain note on the limits of our own method. When our registers disagree with each other, we publish the number we can reconcile and explain why. A figure we cannot stand behind does not go on this site.

Seven people found to need surgery at Kunyami were not handed a referral slip and forgotten. We followed each of them to a hospital in Garki and stayed with them until they recovered. That is what care looks like after the outreach has packed up.

None of it is done alone. The Health Service team runs deworming inside the Academy's summer school. Young people who came to help at an outreach became the next cohort we trained. Doctors, teachers, volunteers and community leaders work as one team, and the community is part of it.

When the budget for Toge was cut mid-planning, the team redesigned the day rather than cancelling it, and reached 196 pupils rather than a handful. In Gosa, young adults bring us ideas for their own community's problems and we fund the best of them. We would rather find a better way than repeat a familiar one.
And we answer for all of it. Every figure we publish can be traced to a named community on a named day, and our trustees review spending and safeguarding every quarter.
We would rather you saw what we value in the work than read it on a wall.
Our team

Our team is small, and most of it works in the field. Clinicians, educators, researchers, communicators and operations staff lead the work in Gosa, Kunyami and Toge, alongside the volunteers they train.
How we are governed
MedWHOLE is overseen by a Board of Trustees and run day to day by the General Coordinator and team leads. Oversight and operations are kept separate.

Every quarter the board reviews what was spent, the results of clinical safety audits, and the safeguarding log. MedWHOLE Alliance for Health and Development is a registered non-profit organisation in Nigeria, Charity ID 169086.

/about/journey.title: The Made Whole Journey
/about/journey.description: MedWHOLE's method, in four phases — engaged, equipped, deployed, supported. How every programme is designed and judged.

blocks.text: The Made Whole Journey
Our method, in four phases. How every MedWHOLE programme is designed, and what we hold each one to.
The Made Whole Journey is how we design and run our work. It is not a path one person walks. It is the sequence every programme is built to follow, and the test we hold each one to.

A programme that engages a community but equips nobody has stopped at the first phase. One that trains people and then leaves them with nowhere to use it has stopped at the second. Naming the four phases lets us say plainly how far a programme has got, and what is still missing.

items: Engaged — we establish presence and meet a real need, free and open to everyone. A medical outreach, a summer school programme, a weekly club.
Equipped — we build skill and character in the same room, over months rather than in a single workshop.
Deployed — people put what they have gained to work in their own community, with us alongside them.
Supported — we stay after the training ends. Grants, mentoring, follow-up, and the next cycle.

blocks.text: Kunyami, February to June 2026

On 14 February 2026 we ran a free medical outreach in Kunyami, a community with no health facility. Five hundred and six people were seen. Among those who helped run it were young people from the community itself, working the registration desk and the service units.

That group became the first cohort of ComPart, our community participation programme. They met fortnightly from February to June, learning graphics and photography, printing and branding, or public health. Every meeting opened with a thirty-minute teaching session.

On 7 June they presented their work — designs, media projects and community advocacy plans. The public health stream then ran Operation Keep Kunyami Clean, a sanitation activity they planned and delivered themselves.
They came as helpers on February 14th. They are now being equipped as leaders.
The Community Innovation Challenge

The Challenge runs all four phases inside a single programme. Young adults from Gosa are recruited, trained for two days, mentored for several weeks, pitch solutions to problems they chose themselves, and the strongest proposals receive grants and continued guidance.

Its curriculum pairs a technical skill with a human one every single day. Prototyping with resourcefulness. Costing with financial literacy. Pitching with public speaking. Deadline pressure with managing stress.

blocks.text: Team and governance
Who does the work, who holds the decisions, and where our policies sit.
Our team

Our team is small, and most of it works in the field. Clinicians, educators, researchers, communicators and operations staff lead the work in Gosa, Kunyami and Toge, alongside the volunteers they train.
Board of Trustees
MedWHOLE is overseen by a Board of Trustees. Every quarter, the board reviews what was spent and on what, the results of clinical safety audits, and the safeguarding log.
The board sets the organisation's direction and holds its leadership to account for delivering it.
How decisions are made
Programme decisions are made by the General Coordinator with the team leads who will carry them out. Every programme has a budget before it runs, and it is approved before money is spent.

We adopt a new community only after spending time there first: a courtesy visit to its leaders, any clearances the work needs, and a first piece of work small enough to learn from. That is how Toge began — a visit to the school in March 2026, clearance from the AMAC Local Education Authority in April, and a school health day in June.
Registration
MedWHOLE Alliance for Health and Development is a registered non-profit organisation in Nigeria, Charity ID 169086.
Our main office is the MedWHOLE Resource Centre, 7 Nissi Drive, Fort Royal, Nnamdi Azikiwe Airport Road, Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja.

/about/accountability.title: Accountability
/about/accountability.description: How MedWHOLE manages funds, reports on its work, and handles complaints.

blocks.text: Accountability
How money is managed, how work is reported, and how to raise a concern.

Every event records what it did on the day. Those records add up to programme totals, programme totals to pillar totals, and pillar totals to the figures on our home page. Nothing is estimated upward.

We publish three separate measures and never add them together. Unique people counts distinct individuals. Attendances counts every visit, which means the same child on four mornings is four attendances and one person. Services counts what was delivered — a deworming dose, a laboratory test, a pair of glasses.

Where our own records disagree, we publish the figure we can reconcile and say so. At Toge in June, our report's column totals did not match its component rows, so this site uses the component sums: 196 pupils screened and 193 dewormed.
How money is managed
Every programme has a budget before it runs, and spending is recorded against it. The Board of Trustees reviews expenditure every quarter.
Money given for a named programme is spent on that programme. A gift that is not designated goes where the need is greatest at the time.
Safeguarding

We work with hundreds of children every week. Written parental consent comes before any medical procedure, refusals are recorded and respected, every facilitator receives a code of conduct, and no child's photograph is published without a parent's written permission.
Raising a concern
If something we have done has gone wrong, we want to know. Write to info@medwhole.org and tell us what happened, where and when.
A concern about the safety of a child or a vulnerable adult goes straight to our Safeguarding Lead at safeguarding@medwhole.org.
Registration

MedWHOLE Alliance for Health and Development is a registered non-profit organisation in Nigeria, Charity ID 169086, based at the MedWHOLE Resource Centre, 7 Nissi Drive, Fort Royal, Nnamdi Azikiwe Airport Road, Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja.

/academy.title: MedWHOLE Academy — free education in Gosa and Kunyami
/academy.description: Free holiday lessons, a weekly club, scholarships and exam coaching for children and teenagers in Gosa and Kunyami — Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja. Open to every child in the community.

blocks.text: MedWHOLE Academy
Whole child. Whole family. Whole community.

Free education for children and teenagers in Gosa and Kunyami. Holiday lessons every August, a club that meets weekly through the year, scholarships for children who had left school, and coaching for the exams that decide what comes next.
Free, and open to every child in the community.
No fees, no uniform requirement, no entrance test. A parent does not need to register in advance, and no child is asked what their family believes.
Five years in Gosa
The Academy began in 2021 at Christ Word Centre in Gosa, with twenty-one children in a weekly club. The first summer school ran that same year.
In August 2026 we taught more than seven hundred children across two communities. On a single Thursday morning that month, 670 children and teenagers were in Summer School classes across both sites.
Gosa and Kunyami
Summer School has run in Gosa every August since 2021. In 2026 it ran in Kunyami for the first time, at the same time, and Good News Club opened there in February.

Kunyami drew 122 children on its first morning and 240 by the fourth. It had not stopped growing when the first week ended. Gosa, in its fifth year, filled to 423 by its second morning and held there.
The two curves say different things and both are useful. One is a programme the community already knows. The other is a programme being discovered.

items: 280 a day at Kunyami, first edition
190 at Good News Club each week
168 at the first Kunyami club meeting

blocks.text: Primary through senior secondary

About forty-three per cent of the children at Gosa Summer School are of secondary-school age. The largest single class band is JSS 1 and 2 — 105 pupils on one morning, more than any primary band on any day.
So the Academy is not only a children's programme, and we have stopped describing it as one. Six class bands run at once every morning, from Primary 1 to SS 3.

items: Summer School — four weeks of free lessons every August, Monday to Thursday mornings. Mathematics, English and reading, plus a skills lab, exams and a closing party.
Good News Club — weekly through the year, in Gosa and Kunyami. Bible lessons, memory verses, songs and activities, with a teenagers' section.
Library and Reading Club — reading support through the year, including guided practice for computer-based exams.
Back-to-School Scholarship — for children who had dropped out, covering the cost of returning.
Exam Coaching — WAEC and JAMB preparation for the senior bands.

blocks.text: How a day is built

A Summer School morning carries mathematics, English and reading, and a memory verse. From the second week a skills lab is added — bead making, soap making, stool making, tote bags, air fresheners. In the final week there are exams, a skills competition, and talks on career, health and mental health.
The Health Service team runs deworming inside the same programme, with written parental consent obtained in advance.
One timetable, carrying reading, a trade, a health check and a conversation about what comes next.
Where a child can go from here

A child who joins Good News Club at seven can move into the teenagers' section, sit in the secondary bands at Summer School, be coached through WAEC, and at eighteen compete in the Community Innovation Challenge with a grant behind their idea.
That path runs across programmes and across years, in one community. It is the reason the Academy is organised as a cluster rather than a set of separate activities.

We publish attendance and unique children separately. 670 is a single morning's attendance across both sites. Gosa's season figure is 450+; Kunyami's 2026 Summer School averaged 280 children a day. Where a figure is a registration count rather than an attendance count, this site says so.
Six class groups need six teachers every morning
Summer School runs six bands at once in Gosa and five in Kunyami. Every one needs a facilitator, every morning, for four weeks.

Four weeks of free lessons every August, in Gosa and Kunyami.

Summer School runs for four weeks every August. Mathematics, English and reading every morning, a memory verse, and from the second week a skills lab in the afternoon. The final week holds exams, a skills and memory verse competition, talks, and a closing party.
It has run in Gosa every year since 2021. In 2026 it ran in Kunyami for the first time, at the same time.

Most of the children who come are on holiday from schools that are overcrowded and short of trained teachers. Four weeks of focused teaching in August is how we help close that gap. Some who come are not in school at all, and for them there is the Back-to-School Scholarship.

blocks.text: Library and Reading Club
Reading support through the year, and guided practice for computer-based exams.

The Reading Club runs outside the August programme, as year-round support. It also provides guided practice on computer-based tests for candidates sitting JAMB — four candidates were supported this way in the second quarter of 2026.
Summer School includes a reading assessment, which is the only literacy measure in our programmes. It means we can report what a child's reading did over four weeks, not only that they attended.
Children and teenagers. Free, and open to every child in the community.
How to join
The Reading Club is free and there is no sign-up. Ask at the Gosa liaison office, Shop 6, Gosa Shopping Complex, for this term's meeting times, or write to info@medwhole.org.

blocks.text: Back-to-School Scholarship
For children who had left school, and what it costs to get them back.

Most of the children at our Summer School programme are on holiday from their own schools. A few are not enrolled anywhere. The scholarship is for them: it covers what it takes to get a child back into school and keep them there.
More than fifty children have gone back to school through the programme since 2021.
Children of school age in Gosa and Kunyami who are out of school. Free, and open to every child in the community.

Some families come to us. Other children we meet through our clubs and our Summer School programme, and find out they are not enrolled anywhere. Either way, we sit down with the family, find out what is keeping the child out of school, and cover what it takes to get them back into a classroom.
Then we stay in touch, because getting a child back is only half of it. Keeping them there is the rest.
To ask about a scholarship, visit the Gosa liaison office, Shop 6, Gosa Shopping Complex, or write to info@medwhole.org.

blocks.text: Our work
Everything we run, and where it is running today.
Three pillars hold the work: health, literacy and empowerment. Under each pillar sit programmes, and under each programme sit dated events that carry their own numbers.
Nutrition is a programme under Health, not a pillar of its own. Health in our terms means physical, mental and systemic wellbeing, and nutrition belongs inside that.
Free care in communities with no health facility, school health screening, nutrition, and follow-up after referral.
Free education for children and teenagers, held mostly within MedWHOLE Academy.
Skills training, mentorship, and a community innovation challenge with grant funding.

sections.label: How we choose where to work

blocks.text: We began in Kyami District, AMAC, along the Nnamdi Azikiwe Airport Road corridor, in communities that sit close to major infrastructure and still have interior sections without basic amenities. Kunyami had no health facility at all.

We start by spending time in a community rather than by delivering to it. Gosa took five years to reach its present scale. Kunyami and Toge began in 2026, and both began with an invitation and a courtesy visit to local leadership.

/our-work/health.title: Health
/our-work/health.description: Free medical outreaches, school health screening, nutrition and follow-up care in Gosa, Kunyami and Toge — Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja.

blocks.text: Health
Physical, mental and systemic wellbeing. We provide care where there is none, and work toward the systems that would make our visits unnecessary.
Kunyami has no health facility. For the people who live there, care has meant travelling elsewhere or going without.

The same pattern repeats along the corridor. Children swim in a river that carries schistosomiasis. Teachers have untreated high blood pressure. Undernutrition in one school we screened was five times more common among boys than girls.

We run free outreaches in communities without facilities, screen children in schools, and follow referred cases through to treatment. We also train community members to carry health knowledge themselves.
We do not treat an outreach as finished on the day. Identifying a case takes a morning; following it through to recovery takes months.

blocks.text: Medical Outreaches
A full day of free care, in communities that have no health facility.

A one-day outreach brings a working clinic to a community that does not have one. Everyone who comes passes through registration and triage, then moves between service units: consultation, laboratory, nursing, eye care, counselling, pharmacy.
What is found on the day does not end on the day. Cases needing more than we can provide are referred to a partner hospital, and we follow them through.
Everyone who comes. Free, and open to everyone in the community.

blocks.text: Continuity of Care
What happens after the outreach packs up.

Continuity of Care is a standing service rather than an event. It covers home follow-up for children needing wound care or treatment for common childhood illness, medical posts kept running during Academy events, and referral tracking from the day a case is identified to the day it is resolved.
Identifying a case takes a morning. Following it through to recovery takes months, and it is the part that decides whether an outreach mattered.
Anyone referred or identified through a MedWHOLE programme. Free, and open to everyone in the community.

blocks.text: School Health Interventions
Health education, screening and deworming, delivered inside the school day.
We take a half-day health programme into a primary school: a general assembly for the whole school, then separate sessions by age and sex, then screening and deworming.
The separate sessions matter. What a six-year-old needs to hear about handwashing is not what a twelve-year-old girl needs to hear about her own safety.
Pupils and teaching staff of the host school. Free, and open to every child in the school.

items: A courtesy visit to school leadership, first
Clearance from the AMAC Local Education Authority
General assembly, then age- and sex-appropriate breakout sessions
Anthropometric screening, and mid-upper arm circumference for under-fives
Albendazole administered under direct observation, with parental consent and recorded refusals
Blood pressure and random blood glucose screening for teaching staff
LEA Primary School, Toge — 30 June 2026. 196 pupils screened, 193 dewormed, 9 teachers screened.

blocks.text: Of 195 pupils with complete measurements, 169 had a normal BMI-for-age. Fourteen were thin and four severely thin. Seven were overweight and one obese.

Undernutrition was five times more common among boys than girls — fifteen cases to three. No pupil presented with an illness needing urgent treatment on the day. One teacher was referred for high blood pressure.
Nutritional status was assessed using BMI-for-Age Z-score, the standard the World Health Organization recommends for school-age children.

One limitation is worth stating. Exact dates of birth were not recorded, so each child's age was estimated at the midpoint of their stated year. The figures are a close approximation rather than an exact clinical score, and we are capturing dates of birth from now on.
Three parents declined deworming for their children. The refusals were recorded and the children were not treated.

The work has three parts: screening children to find who is affected, targeted support for those who are, and community feeding where need is widespread.

blocks.text: Literacy
Reading, learning and the skills that follow from them. Most of this work sits inside MedWHOLE Academy.

Schools in these communities are overcrowded and short of trained teachers. A child can go through a whole term without the attention they need, and many fall behind in reading. Summer School fills that gap during the holidays. A smaller number of children are not in school at all, and the Back-to-School Scholarship exists for them.
It reaches past childhood. When we ran our first skills cohort for young adults in Kunyami, the thing that most shaped how we had to teach was the literacy level of the participants.

We teach free, in the community, and in the holidays when school is out. We measure reading rather than only counting attendance, and we return the same programme to the same community year after year.
The work is held almost entirely within MedWHOLE Academy, which has its own page.

Agency, leadership and the practical capacity to act. We train the people already doing the work.
Young adults in these communities are not short of willingness. They are short of training, equipment and a route from willing to employed.
The volunteers who ran the registration desk at our February outreach in Kunyami are the clearest example. They gave a day of skilled work and had nowhere to take it next.
We recruit from the people who already turn up, train them in a marketable skill over months rather than days, and stay with them after the training ends.

blocks.text: Community Innovation Challenge
Ideas that heal.
Young adults in Gosa choose a problem in their own community, and we back them to solve it. Training, mentors, and grants for the strongest proposals.

The Challenge runs over several weeks. Participants are recruited from the community, trained across a two-day bootcamp, mentored through prototyping and pitching, and then present to judges and the community. The strongest proposals receive grants.
We do not arrive with the problem list. Participants assess their own community and choose what to work on, within three tracks.

items: A member of the Gosa community
Has an idea for making the community better, or is simply passionate about it

blocks.text: Free, and open to everyone in the community. You do not need to arrive with a team — teams are formed on the first day of the bootcamp.

All three are health problems, which is why a health alliance runs an innovation challenge. Participants are not delivering health services. They are solving the problems we otherwise treat clinically.

Every day pairs a hard skill with a human one.

/impact.title: Impact
/impact.description: What MedWHOLE has done in Gosa, Kunyami and Toge — Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja — with dates, methods and the figures behind each claim.

blocks.text: Impact
Every figure here is dated, sourced, and traceable to a named community on a named day.

items: 506 people seen in one day in a community with no clinic — Kunyami, 14 February 2026
670 children and teenagers in class on one morning — both sites, August 2026

blocks.text: At Kunyami on 14 February 2026 we saw 506 people in a single day: 274 children and 232 adults. The community has no health facility, so for most of them this was the first consultation available to them in their own village.
The day produced 697 clinical services — 450 deworming treatments, 136 laboratory investigations, 39 electrocardiograms, 47 eye consultations and 25 pairs of medicated glasses.
At Toge on 30 June, 196 pupils were screened and 193 dewormed. Eighteen were undernourished. One teacher was referred for high blood pressure.
In August 2026, more than 700 children and teenagers attended free Summer School across two communities. On the Thursday of the first week, 670 were in class at once.
Good News Club began with twenty-one children in 2021. Three hundred and five were present at its fifth anniversary in February 2026.
More than fifty children have returned to school through the Back-to-School Scholarship since 2021.

Twelve people completed the first ComPart cohort between February and June 2026, across three learning streams. The public health stream delivered eight sessions and then planned and ran a community sanitation project.
The first Community Innovation Challenge ran in Gosa in August 2026. Its outcomes are being compiled.
2026: the same model, a second community
Good News Club and Summer School were both built in Gosa over five years. In 2026 both opened in Kunyami.

Good News Club Kunyami drew 168 children to its first meeting on 6 February. Summer School Kunyami drew 122 on its first morning in August and 240 by its fourth — fifty-six per cent of what Gosa reaches in its fifth year, inside one week.
Five years proving it in one community. One year moving it into the next.

blocks.text: We publish three measures and never add them together.
Unique people counts distinct individuals. Attendances counts visits — the same child on four mornings is four attendances and one person. Services counts what was delivered.

Where our own records disagree, we publish the figure we can reconcile and say which one it is. At Toge, our report's column totals did not match its component rows, so this site uses the component sums: 196 screened and 193 dewormed.

One measurement limitation is worth naming. Nutritional status at Toge was assessed using BMI-for-Age Z-score, the WHO standard for school-age children, but exact dates of birth were not on record, so each child's age was taken at the midpoint of their stated year. The figures are a close approximation. We are capturing dates of birth from now on.

/communities/gosa.title: Gosa
/communities/gosa.description: MedWHOLE's first community. Free education, health outreaches and a community innovation challenge in Gosa, Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja, since 2021.

blocks.text: Gosa
Our first community, and where everything was built.

Gosa is a farming settlement of around four thousand people on the Nnamdi Azikiwe Airport Road, in Kyami District, AMAC. It sits at the edge of a fast-growing part of Abuja, close to major infrastructure, and the interior streets have very little of it.

When we started working here in 2021, quality healthcare and schooling were hard to reach, housing was poor, potable water was limited, and there was almost no waste collection — including along the stream much of the community draws from.
Five years on, Gosa is where most of what MedWHOLE does was first built and proved it worked.
MedWHOLE Academy began here, with twenty-one children in a church hall in 2021.

A Good News Club and a reading club now meet weekly, giving children somewhere to read and ask questions outside school hours. Every August, free Summer School runs for the whole month: mathematics, English and reading each morning, and a skills lab where children learn a trade they can actually use. In 2026 it taught more than four hundred and fifty.

items: 190 at Good News Club each week

blocks.text: We run free outreaches in Gosa, treat what can be treated on the day, follow up the people who need checking on, and refer what needs a hospital.

The following-up is the part that decides whether an outreach mattered. We are now working toward sustained health provision for Gosa and the settlements around it, rather than returning with a tent every few months.

The Community Innovation Challenge belongs to Gosa. Young adults from the community are screened, placed in teams, and supported by facilitators to take an idea from a problem they have noticed to a costed solution they can present — waste management, water access, maternal and child health.
They are not asked to comment on their community's problems. They choose which one to work on, and they build the answer.

In Gosa, MedWHOLE is a household name — for the reading clubs, the summer school, the outreaches and the innovation challenge, and for what has happened to the children and young adults who have been through them.
Twenty-one children in a church hall. More than four hundred at Summer School five years later.
Join our work in Gosa

There is always something here that needs doing. Teach a Summer School band in August. Facilitate a team through the innovation challenge. Bring a clinical skill to an outreach. Sponsor a pillar for a year, or write to us and we will tell you plainly what is short.

/communities/kunyami.title: Kunyami
/communities/kunyami.description: Free education, health outreaches and skills training in Kunyami, Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja. Our second community, since February 2026.

blocks.text: Kunyami
Where we found out whether any of this works anywhere else.

Kunyami is a short distance from Gosa, on the same Airport Road, in the same district. It is a farming community of more than three thousand people, built on sloping ground with poor roads, and a large share of its population are children and young people.

It has no health facility. Care has meant travelling elsewhere or going without, and most households have no potable water, which shows up in the water-borne infections we see. Non-communicable disease is on record here too. Schooling is hard for children and young people to hold on to.
We came in February 2026 with programmes we had already spent five years building in Gosa.

Our first day here was a free medical outreach on 14 February 2026. Five hundred and six people were seen: registration and triage, then consultation, laboratory, nursing, eye care, counselling and pharmacy.

Seven people were found to need surgery. All seven were referred to Gibonna Women's Hospital in Garki, all seven were operated on, and all seven recovered without complications. That chain — outreach to referral to recovery — is what we mean by following through.
We are working toward sustained, accessible provision here rather than periodic visits.
Good News Club opened in Kunyami on 6 February 2026 and drew 168 children on its first Friday. Summer School followed in August, the first time it had ever run outside Gosa.

It started with 122 children on the Monday and reached 240 by the Thursday, and it kept climbing — across the month it averaged 280 a day. Children who had fallen behind were given study support, which has made going back to class easier to sustain.

items: 280 a day at the first Summer School

blocks.text: The young people from Kunyami who worked the service units at the February outreach became the first ComPart cohort. They met fortnightly from February to June, training in graphics and media, printing and branding, or public health.
Twelve completed it. At the graduation they presented work they can show to a client, and the public health stream went on to plan and run a community sanitation project themselves.
Good News Club and Summer School were both built in Gosa over five years. Both opened in Kunyami inside twelve months, and both worked immediately.
That is the answer to the question anyone funding scale asks first: does this work anywhere other than where you built it.
Five years proving it in one community. One year moving it into the next.
Join our work in Kunyami

Kunyami is a year old and growing faster than anything we have run before. It needs teachers each August, facilitators for the next ComPart cohort, clinical volunteers for the outreaches, and funding for a community that still has no health facility of its own.

/communities/toge.title: Toge
/communities/toge.description: School health, screening and deworming in Toge, Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja. Our newest community, since June 2026.

blocks.text: Toge
Our newest community. We are at the beginning here.
Toge is about the same size as Gosa — more than a thousand households, around four people to a home, so roughly four thousand people in all. Most of them are women and children.
There are a few primary schools and no secondary school, so a child who finishes primary here has nowhere in the community to go next. There is no hospital serving the settlement.
We have run outreaches in Toge, and in June 2026 we took a full health programme into LEA Primary School: a general assembly, then separate sessions by age and sex, then screening and deworming.

One hundred and ninety-six pupils were screened and 193 dewormed. Eighteen were undernourished, five times more often among boys than girls. Nine teachers were screened and one was referred for high blood pressure.

The older girls' session covered hygiene and how to identify, resist and report abuse. The boys' session covered hygiene, safe toilet practice, and the risks of swimming in the river — drowning, and the schistosomiasis we had already found in neighbouring Kunyami.

We are talking to the people who hold things together here — school leadership, the local education authority, community leaders — about what a longer presence should look like. Water, sanitation, hygiene and river safety are the priorities on record.
We would rather agree that with Toge than arrive with a plan.
Join our work in Toge

Toge is the community where you can still shape what we do, because very little of it is fixed. We are working out with its leaders what a longer presence should look like, and water, sanitation, hygiene and river safety are the priorities on record.
A partner or volunteer who comes in now helps set the direction rather than staffing a plan that already exists.

blocks.text: School Health Intervention — Toge
30 June 2026 · LEA Primary School, Toge, Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja · Completed
A general assembly for the whole school, then separate sessions by age and sex, then screening and deworming.

The younger pupils covered handwashing, bathing, tooth brushing and basic nutrition. Older boys covered personal hygiene, safe toilet practice and the risks of swimming in the river — drowning and schistosomiasis. Older girls covered personal hygiene, toilet safety, oral hygiene, and how to identify, resist and report abuse or threats.
Free, and open to every child in the school.

Undernutrition was five times more common among boys than girls — fifteen cases to three. No pupil presented with an illness needing urgent treatment on the day. Localised skin lesions and probable fungal scalp infections were observed.
One teacher, a woman of 49, had moderately elevated blood pressure. She was counselled and referred to the Primary Health Centre in Kuje, where she lives.

Nutritional status was assessed using BMI-for-Age Z-score, the standard the World Health Organization recommends for school-age children. Exact dates of birth were not on record, so each child's age was taken at the midpoint of their stated year. The figures are a close approximation rather than an exact clinical score.

A courtesy visit to school leadership in March 2026, clearance from the AMAC Local Education Authority in April, then a pause during a teachers' union strike. The programme resumed after it was resolved, under a new head teacher.

The budget was reduced during planning. Individual clinical consultations were dropped and the team moved to tiered health education with screening — which is how 196 pupils were reached rather than a fraction of them.

blocks.text: ComPart Pioneer Cohort Graduation
7 June 2026 · Kunyami, Kyami District, AMAC, FCT Abuja · Completed

The first ComPart cohort finished where it had been heading since February: presenting work. Graduates showed designs, media projects and community advocacy frameworks they had built across the programme.

The cohort had come straight out of the 14 February medical outreach in the same community. They met fortnightly from February to June across three streams — graphics and media, printing and branding, and public health.
The public health stream planned and ran Operation Keep Kunyami Clean, a sanitation activity in their own community.
The next phase takes ComPart into other Airport Road communities, with training adapted to participants' reading levels and working hours.

/safeguarding.title: Safeguarding
/safeguarding.description: How MedWHOLE protects the children and vulnerable adults in its programmes, and how to report a concern.

blocks.text: Safeguarding
We work with hundreds of children every week. This is how we protect them.
More than seven hundred children and teenagers attended our Summer School programme in August 2026. Protecting them is a condition of running the programmes at all, not an add-on to them.
Every child and vulnerable adult who takes part in a MedWHOLE programme, and every member of staff, facilitator, volunteer and partner who works with them.

items: Written parental consent before any medical intervention involving a child. Before deworming at Summer School in August 2026, consent forms went to the families of every child across both sites.
Refusals are recorded and respected. At the Toge school health intervention in June, three parents declined deworming for their children. The refusals were logged and the children were not treated.
A code of conduct for facilitators, delivered at the start of every programme. The Community Innovation Challenge covered it on the first day of its bootcamp.

Age- and sex-appropriate teaching. At Toge, older girls were taught personal hygiene and how to identify, resist and report abuse or threats. Older boys were taught hygiene, safe toilet practice and the risks of swimming in the river.
Sex education and health hygiene inside Summer School, taught in separate age bands.
Photography consent. No image of a child is published without written consent from a parent or guardian.

sections.label: If you are worried about a child

blocks.text: If you are worried about a child
Tell us straight away. Anyone can raise a concern — a parent, a child, a volunteer, a teacher or a neighbour. If a child is in immediate danger, contact the police first.
Every report is acknowledged within two hours. We then make sure the child is safe, refer to medical or statutory services where that is needed, and bring in the board's safeguarding trustee.
